[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: everyday counting starts at 1 (first = number 1), maths subscripts a_1..a_n run from 1, and f(i) with parentheses means 'apply to i'. Java rule: a[i] uses square brackets and is 0-origin, so the first element is a[0] and the last is a[a.length-1].
[1] misconception (M) -> IndexIsValue: wrong rule: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value. Right rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.
[2] misconception (M) -> ArrayIndexStartsAtOne: wrong rule: The first element of a is a[1]. Right rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
[3] misconception (M) -> ArrayRangeInclusive: wrong rule: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive. Right rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.
[4] misconception (M) -> ArrayAccessWithParentheses: wrong rule: a(i) accesses element i of an array. Right rule: Array elements are selected with square brackets, a[i]; a(i) would be a call of a method named a.
[5] misconception (M) -> ArrayElementNotVariable: wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.
[6] misconception (M) -> ElementNameIsWholeArray: wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The array is a (a[] in the book); a[i] is the single element at index i.
[7] misconception (M) -> ElementBoundToOldIndex: wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is executed.
[8] inconsistent_trace (T) -> IndexIsValue: Points to LT: in a[i], a is evaluated, then i with its current value, then the bounds check, then the element is read or written. Inconsistent application: i is updated on one line, but a later a[i] is traced with the old i. (here mixing in: "i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value")
[9] misconception (M) -> ArrayUseScansAllCells: wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: an array access expression; a[i] names the single element variable at position i of the array a refers to.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: the index is any int-valued expression in square brackets; the valid indices of an array of length n are 0 to n-1, and an access outside that range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: the array reference is evaluated before the index; the index expression is fully evaluated with current variable values; the bounds are checked; then the element is fetched or, on the left of =, becomes the target. In a[i] = a[j], the target a[i] is located before a[j] is read.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: a[i] has the element type and the value currently stored at position i. For int[] a = {5, 7, 9}, a[1] is 7 and a[0] + a[2] is 14.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: reading a[i] changes nothing. a[i] = v changes only element i (i, a and all other elements are unchanged), and a[i]++ adds 1 to that one element.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): An element can be indexed only after the array is created, and the n given to new sets the valid indices 0..n-1.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A traversal uses the loop variable as the index, so the same expression a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Every index value is checked against 0 and a.length at run time; any other value throws.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): a[i] on a 2-D array yields row i (itself a 1-D array), and a[i][j] then indexes into that row.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): The exchange reads and writes elements only through their indices: t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): A lookup table uses a data value as the index (months[m]), so the data must lie in 0..length-1.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
[7] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: random access, reaching any element directly by its position in constant time (address plus index), so code touches only the elements it needs.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> IndexIsValue: Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: index when you need a particular element by position, or when the position is computed from data (counts[score]++, months[m]). When every value is processed in order and the position is never needed, an enhanced for loop is simpler.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The index must be in 0..a.length-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: index < 0 or >= a.length, e.g. a[a.length], a[i+1] on the last pass, a[i-1] at i = 0, a[0] of an empty array (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The index must have type int (after promotion); long or double indices are rejected. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a[1.5], a[x] with double x, or a[n] with long n (incompatible types: possible lossy conversion)
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Elements are selected with brackets, not parentheses. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a(i) is written for a[i] (cannot find symbol: method a)
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An index is a position, not the stored value. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: code uses i where a[i] is meant (or a[i] where i is meant), e.g. returning i as the maximum value or comparing positions instead of contents

An array must be created with new before any of its elements a[i] can be accessed.
The values listed in braces are stored at indices 0, 1, 2, ... in order, and a[i] reads the value at index i.
Valid indexes run from 0 to a.length - 1; any other index throws an exception when it is used.
An exchange reads and writes a[i] and a[j] by index.
A traversal uses the loop variable i as the index, so a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
A lookup table is read by index, a[i].
Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
Saved values are read back by index, H[i], instead of being recomputed.
A 1-D array uses one index a[i]; a 2-D array uses two, a[i][j], where the first index chooses the row array.
